newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Allies said to back Zaire army in widening war.
newsitem.headline: Allies said to back Zaire army in widening war.

text.p: Zaire expects troops from Morocco, Togo and Chad to help its army contain a rebel campaign that has spread to the mineral-producing Shaba Province, a senior Zaire defence ministry official said on Monday.
"Togo, Morocco and Chad are all prepared to send troops along with materials. Egypt has offered materials mostly to equip the infantry," the official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"The planes for this operation have already been chartered," the official said. He could not give a definite date for the arrival of the foreign troops.
Tutsi-led rebels battling the Zaire army since October have extended their campaign and territory they hold from the borders of Rwanda and Uganda to Zaire's mineral-rich Shaba Province.
If the fall of the lake-side Shaba town of Kalemie is confirmed, the border strip under rebel control would have stretched for over 1,000 km (600 miles).
A defence official said earlier the army was battling to hold on to Kalemie. Rebel and military sources said the interior port town had already fallen.

Zaire accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of fighting along with ethnic Tutsis who launched an armed rebellion after local authorities threatened to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda. Rebel leaders now say their objective is to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko who has ruled Zaire since 1965.
Mobutu, who has been convalescing in France from cancer surgery, arrived in Morocco for a three-day visit and talks with long-time ally King Hassan expected to centre on the fighting.
Asked about the foreign troops, the chief of protocol for Mobutu's delegation, Iema Mena, said: "I don't know. I cannot comment on this report from Kinshasa, I am now in Rabat."

Moroccan troops helped put down a 1977 secessionist uprising in Shaba after Zairean forces were overwhelmed. They also relieved French and Belgian paratroops backing Zairean authorities in the mining town of Kolwezi the following year.
The defence official said Zaire had started a nationwide recruitment campaign for the army to train up 13 rapid intervention commando brigades of 2,000 men each.

Siganalling the widening international scope of the conflict in the heart of Africa, the official added that China and Israel would help train the commandos at bases in the Zaire provinces of Shaba, Upper Zaire and Equateur.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt ruled out the intervention of France, which campaigned unsuccessfully last year for foreign intervention in Zaire. "There is no
question of that...There are only five French soldiers in Zaire protecting the embassy in Kinshasa," he told reporters.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette met his Zairean counterpart Kamanda Wa Kamanda in Paris on Monday but the ministry said they would not talk to the press.

France expressed concern last Friday at signs that "elements" from Uganda and Rwanda were participating in the fighting in eastern Zaire but said it had no proof that regular army units from those countries were involved.

"Since last night there has been heavy fighting in the northern part of Kalemie," the defence official told Reuters. "The FAZ (Zaire army) controls it but reinforcements are having to be sent in from the military base at Kamina."
The town, about 800 km (500 miles) on a crumbling road to the provincial capital Lubumbashi, is still a long way away from Shaba's copper and cobalt mining heartland.

But military and political sources said even a tiny foothold on a corner of Shaba could raise the chances of the province's rebellious leaders siding with the guerrillas. That would minimise the need for rebels to fight their way through.
